# Tannehill Precision



## The project: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- The automated cell
- The three old machines
- Tax on the sale of the old machines
- Depreciation tax shields
- Salvage, year 8
:::

## The savings: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Operators
- Scrap
- Maintenance
- Floor space
- Plant overhead
- The rebuild of the manual cells
:::


## Takeaways {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[A project is a comparison]{.card-title}

Name the counterfactual before you name a number: what happens if we don't do it?
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Opportunity cost]{.card-title}

Not zero because you own it, and not the accounting charge. It is the cash the
resource would earn in its next best use.
:::


::: {.card .card-sand}
[Allocations are averages]{.card-title}

Charge the project what changes. Sometimes that is less than the allocation.
Sometimes it is more.
:::

:::

# Kestrel Pet Nutrition

## Read {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Ten minutes. Upload to lab648, tell AI to read it, and chat with AI if you want.
:::

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[The proposal]{.card-title}

Refrigerated capacity, five years of forecast revenue.
:::


::: {.card}
[The details]{.card-title}

Spending, overhead, and timing.
:::
:::

## The investment: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Refrigerated capacity and cold-chain equipment
- Depreciation tax shields
- Working capital
- The equipment sale, year 5
- Tax on the equipment sale
:::

## The operations: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Fresh line contribution
- Lost kibble contribution
- Incremental fixed cash costs
- Corporate overhead allocation
- Consumer research and formulation
:::


## Build it {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Fifteen minutes. Upload to lab648, tell AI to read it, and ask AI to help build the analysis if you want.
:::

::: {.steps}
1. Year 3 under both cannibalization assumptions
2. All five years, with working capital and the after-tax equipment sale
3. NPV under each assumption
:::


## Takeaways {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Sunk costs]{.card-title}

Money already spent does not enter the analysis.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Cannibalization]{.card-title}

When a project takes revenue from an existing product, the loss is that
product's cash flow.
:::

::: {.card}
[Allocations are averages]{.card-title}

Charge the project what changes — which is sometimes less than the
allocation and sometimes more.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Working capital is a change]{.card-title}

You fund the increase, not the level, and you get it back at the end.
:::

::: {.card}
[Tax schedules outlive projects]{.card-title}

A depreciation schedule set by statute does not stop when your forecast does.
The gap is what makes a disposal taxable.
:::

::: {.card .card-sage}
[Find the threshold]{.card-title}

A breakeven turns an argument about beliefs into a question about evidence.
:::
:::

## A Quick Case {.plain-title}


Dunmore Brewing launches a hard seltzer at $40 million of revenue. Research says 60
percent of the volume comes out of a competitor's seltzer, 15 percent out of
Dunmore's own light lager, and 25 percent is new to the category. The light
lager carries a 44 percent contribution margin.

::: {.incremental}
- How much should Dunmore charge the seltzer project for cannibalization?
- Should Dunmore be pleased or worried that most of the volume comes from a
  rival?
:::

## Another Quick Case {.plain-title}


Ivara distributes packaged food to convenience stores from one leased warehouse.
Warehouse cost is collected in a pool and charged to product lines at $14.00 per
pallet shipped — $5.60 of occupancy, $8.40 of handling labor and equipment.

A proposed dry goods line would ship 40,000 pallets a year, so the model carries
a $560,000 warehouse charge. The warehouse has been full for two years and the
lease is fixed. The line's inventory would go to a third-party facility, 3,000
pallet positions at $210 a position, worked by Ivara's own crews.

::: {.incremental}
- Occupancy of the existing building: when, and how much?
- Third-party space: when, and how much?
- Handling labor: when, and how much?
- What should the line be charged for warehousing?
- Would your answer change if the warehouse had room to spare?
:::


# Kinnaird Mills

## Read {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Ten minutes. A combined heat and power retrofit at a paper mill.  Use AI if you want.
:::


## When, how much, and in whose dollars? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- The turbine and heat recovery generator
- Depreciation deductions
- Displaced energy
- The service contract
:::


## What did you assume? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Rasch's arithmetic checks out. Do you agree with his conclusion?
- Suppose inflation ran well above expectations for fifteen years. What happens
  to a project like this one?
- Rasch wrote "revisit if gas moves." What would you send back to him?
:::

## Build it {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. The project in nominal terms, escalating what escalates
2. The same project in real terms, agreeing to the dollar
3. Rasch's version alongside, for the difference
4. The gas price at which the project fails
:::

## Walk us through it {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Screens up.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Put your two versions side by side.
- Take us through the service contract row in each.
- Then the depreciation row.
:::

## Takeaways {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Market rates are nominal]{.card-title}

A discount rate built from observed yields and premiums already contains
expected inflation. It cannot be paired with cash flows that do not.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[A flat price is a forecast]{.card-title}

Holding a number at today's level is a claim that the real price falls every
year.
:::

::: {.card}
[Consistency, not preference]{.card-title}

Real and nominal both work and must agree to the dollar. Only the mixture is
wrong.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Divide, do not subtract]{.card-title}

The real rate is the nominal over inflation, minus one. The shortcut is close
at 2 percent and far off at 40.
:::

::: {.card}
[Some amounts are fixed in nominal terms]{.card-title}

Signed contracts, statutory deductions, fixed-rate debt, dollar covenants. In a
real model, each of them has to be deflated.
:::

::: {.card .card-sage}
[Inflation and the depreciation shield]{.card-title}

Depreciation is set in the dollars of the purchase date and deducted in later,
cheaper ones. Higher inflation lowers the real value of the shield, which
matters most for capital-intensive projects.
:::
:::

# Halloran Dairy

## Read {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Eight minutes. Both papers recommend the same plant. They disagree only about
how much of it to build.
:::

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Build it now]{.card-title}

Three lines, $36 million, ready for the season.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Stage it]{.card-title}

One line, $18 million, and a decision in two years that costs $4 million more
to keep open.
:::
:::

## Build it now: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Three lines, year 0
- Depreciation tax shields
- EBITDA, years 1 and 2
- EBITDA from year 3, in each state
- Salvage, year 8, in each state
:::

## Stage it: when, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- One line, year 0
- EBITDA, years 1 and 2
- The decision itself
- The second and third lines
- Depreciation tax shields on each tranche
- Salvage, year 8, and the book value still left on the expansion
:::

## What did you assume? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- When does Halloran have to commit to the second and third lines, and does your
  model let it use what it knows by then?
- Staging buys the right to expand. How much of the staged path is the line, and
  how much is the right?
- How sure about the bid would you have to be before building everything now?
:::

## Build it {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. Build It Now, valued in each state and then combined
2. Stage It, working backward from the two choices at year 2
3. The difference, and what it says about the $4 million
4. The probability at which the two paths are equal
:::

## Walk us through it {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Screens up.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Take us through your decision node and what sits on each branch.
- Then the branch you rejected, and what it was worth.
- Give us your recommendation and what would change it.
:::

## Takeaways {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[A future choice is not a forecast]{.card-title}

You do not forecast what you will do. You value the right to decide later, with
information you do not have now.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Value at the node, then discount]{.card-title}

Work backward. Take the maximum at each decision date, and carry that back.
:::

::: {.card}
[Order matters]{.card-title}

Take expectations before the decision and you have assumed the decision is made
without knowing which state occurred.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Most of it is the option]{.card-title}

The line itself barely clears. Four fifths of the staged path is the right to
decide in 2028.
:::

::: {.card}
[An option is not a fixed amount]{.card-title}

The expansion right grows as success becomes likelier and shrinks toward nothing
as it recedes. Quote it with the probability it was computed at.
:::

::: {.card .card-sage}
[When staging is worth paying for]{.card-title}

If you are confident, build everything rather than pay to keep the decision
open.
:::
:::

# Brannock Chemicals

## Read {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Eight minutes. A $310 million specialty resin plant on the Gulf Coast.
:::

::: {.note}
Approved by the capital committee in September. Rebuilt by an analyst preparing
the board paper.
:::

## When, and how much? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- The plant
- Depreciation tax shields
- Contribution: price, volume, variable cost
- Fixed cash costs
:::

## And how uncertain? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Which of those items is known, and which is not?
- For the ones that are not: how much do they vary?
- Do they vary together?
- Who at Brannock is in a position to answer that?
:::

## What did you assume? {.plain-title}

::: {.incremental}
- Run it at three correlations. What did you find?
- Which of your statistics moved most? Which moved least?
- Which of them belongs in the board paper?
- What else did the AI decide for you when it built this?
:::

## Build it {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. The deterministic base case, year by year
2. The simulation at zero correlation, five statistics
3. The same at +0.65 and −0.65
4. The one number you would put in the board paper, and why
:::

## Walk us through it {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Screens up.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Take us through how you drew the inputs.
- Then your three columns of statistics.
- Tell us which one you are reporting, and what it would mean for Brannock.
:::

## Takeaways {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[A point estimate is a distribution]{.card-title}

A single column states that every input is known.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[The base case is not the mean]{.card-title}

The value at the average input is not the average value. Wherever the model
multiplies uncertain things together, the two differ.
:::

::: {.card}
[One at a time is not uncertainty]{.card-title}

Moving each input alone holds every other input at its base value. Things that
go wrong tend to go wrong together.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Correlation is a claim]{.card-title}

It is an assertion about what drives the business, and it comes from people who
know the industry, not from the model.
:::

::: {.card}
[Pick the statistic deliberately]{.card-title}

The mean, the median and the fifth percentile answer different questions. Report
the one that matches the consequence you face.
:::

::: {.card .card-sage}
[Something chose the defaults]{.card-title}

Every model contains assumptions nobody made on purpose.
:::
:::
